subtopic: NATO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: NATO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to
direct a question to the right hon. Prime Minister. In view of the growing embarrassment to our representatives at NATO and to
members of parliament arising from the ambiguity of his government's position toward NATO and the resulting disrepute of this country, can the Prime Minister reconsider his position and give the house an assurance that the study of our external position will be completed by an early date, which he might indicate, to be followed promptly by a firm statement by the Prime Minister as to what our policy is?

subtopic: NATO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with regard to the so-called growing embarrassment mentioned by the hon. gentleman, I should like to reassure him that this is not the case. Our position is as I described it in the house a few days ago. Of course when the review is completed I will want to make a statement about the government's policy in that area, but until that time has come the government will continue to assume the present position.

subtopic: NATO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question. In view of the obvious refusal of the Prime Minister to give any firm commitment with regard to the time of completion of this study, would the Prime Minister indicate whether the study is being conducted simply within the governmental spheres or whether personnel outside the government service is being consulted in connection with it?

subtopic: NATO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, let me answer once again the first part of the hon. gentleman's question in this way. It is not that I refuse to give assurance with regard to the date, but that such a date does not exist, and of course I am not in a position to say now when the study will be completed. We want it to be well and thoroughly done, and we realize that the sooner it is completed the better. I cannot give a date for reasons not under my control; we want this study to be as thorough as possible.
With regard to the second part of the question, I just want to say that the review is being done in a way which we find to be most compatible with a fresh and new look being given to this subject in the advice to the government.

subtopic: NATO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, is it really too much to ask the Prime Minister on a question
2720	COMMONS
Inquiries of the Ministry as important as this one to give us an indication as to the scope of the review and the scope of the consultation in connection with the review?

subtopic: NATO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have no hesitation in answering the hon. gentleman with regard to the scope of the review. It is very wide in scope; that is why it is taking some time. I believe I have indicated at another time in the house that it extends to our external policy both in Europe-

subtopic: NATO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: But, Mr. Speaker-

subtopic: NATO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: This is the scope of the review.

subtopic: NATO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: What about the scope of the consultation?

subtopic: NATO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: The scope of the consultation is as wide as is the subject. The Department of External Affairs is itself engaged in this review with the help of all people necessary to ensure the best possible results. Most of the study is being done within the department, but the government is also turning to other sources of advice.

subtopic: NATO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: I have a further supplementary question. Could the Prime Minister indicate whether the representatives of his government, the Canadian personnel at the NATO meeting, are giving any assurance to NATO countries with regard to the continuation of the stationing of the Canadian armed forces in Europe; and if any such assurance is being given, is the actual size of the forces to be maintained under NATO also indicated and for what if any length of time?

subtopic: NATO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the two ministers engaged in the Brussels talks now are telling our fellow members of NATO that we are engaged in this review; that at the present time we do not want to make any decisions which will prejudge the results. We are not envisaging now any drastic move forward or backward out of NATO until this review is completed. We are trying as much as possible to hold the line until the review is completed.

subtopic: NATO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
I have one final supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, on a question of such importance. Is it fair to assume from what the Prime Minister has said that the representatives of Canada at this council meeting will not in fact give any firm assurance with regard to the forces, as to quantity or as to time?

DEBATES	November 14, 1968

subtopic: NATO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: Well, it depends what the hon. member intends by that type of assurance. We of course are not going to give any firm assurance in respect of increasing our commitments to NATO; neither are our representatives instructed to indicate we are going to pull out of NATO. I hope this answers the question.

subtopic: NATO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I should like to ask the Prime Minister if he made a determination as to the accuracy of reports that our ambassador to NATO has denounced Canada's NATO policy as being vacillating?

subtopic: NATO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, I have not attempted to determine that. I take the position that in this particular government, policy is decided by the cabinet and not by the press.
Right Kon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince
Albert): May I ask the Prime Minister, then, why he is getting this information outside of cabinet circles and outside the Department of External Affairs, and why he does not tell us who are these anonymities who give advice to the Canadian government about what it ought to do?

subtopic: NATO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the policy decisions of this government are based on advice not only from civil servants but from all the areas which are available to us. This government is not taking the position that it must necessarily be guided only by what is decided by the civil servants. We are ministers who are responsible to the Canadian people and we are seeking advice from all possible sources.

subtopic: NATO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: I do not intend to embarrass the Prime Minister by pressing the question, but who are these incognitos who are being consulted about what Canada should do in connection with a policy that Canadians as a whole support?

subtopic: NATO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it would not be realistic to expect me to give the names of all the people who have given me advice over the past year. They would probably include the right hon. member.

subtopic: NATO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: All I have to say is that if I were consulted I would advise carrying out Canada's responsibilities, which this government is not even doing.

subtopic: NATO-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:

maintopic: REPRESENTATIONS AS TO CANADIAN HOLDINGS OF U.S. FUNDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the matter has been discussed, and it is a question of continuing discussion. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think the government is restricted by the present level of the ceiling. We are close to the ceiling now. speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: REPRESENTATIONS AS TO CANADIAN HOLDINGS OF U.S. FUNDS

Mr. Speaker, in taking part in the third reading stage of Bill No. C-124 I should like to support the views expressed by hon. members on both sides of the house concerning the need for the best type of service at the lowest possible cost by our national transportation system, the C.N.R. I particularly support the representations made by hon. members from Newfoundland and the city of Winnipeg.
It is my submission that railways, by their very nature, are public utilities and should operate first and foremost as public services. The public and national interests must take precedence over the narrow interests of a particular railway company. Let me say at the outset that I have always felt the C.N.R. is a great transportation system and is doing a better job than most railway systems throughout the world. In my opinion the C.N.R. is doing a better job of serving the public of Canada than the privately owned system.
I for one would be much happier if this bill provided for several hundred million dollars more to allow the minister to commence to purchase and nationalize the other major railway company in Canada. As one who spent 15 years as a railway employee, watching the disintegration and discontinuance of the services railways must give the public, I submit that the new federal government must move toward a national transportation policy that will provide for an integrated transportation system which is rational, efficient and serves the people of the nation at the lowest possible cost. The public need for railway transportation service takes priority over private needs. If, for example, the choice is between passenger service needed by the people of Newfoundland or dollars, surely the choice is easily made. The people of that area must take priority over dollars.

Recently the Post Office Department talked of profit and efficiency to justify the increase in postal rates. If one tries to satisfy a certain area from a political point of view, there is obviously dissatisfaction in another. I will now deal with the Canadian National. First I will deal with the material situation of the company as far as the line between Quebec City, Abitibi and Cochrane, in Ontario, is concerned. As 250 miles of that line are in the riding of Champlain and that it is the only means available to me to get out of there-since there is no road suitable for motor vehicles-I often travel by train. The situation on the train is sometimes so ridiculous, so absurd that we may wonder whether the administrators are responsible.
For instance, I am told-though I am not given official statistics-that the operation of this line is uneconomic. That is hard to understand, if one considers, as I noticed it myself, as well as the citizens of the area, that the train on the Quebec City-Abitibi-Cochrane is always packed.
In fact, the last two times I travelled on that train, I had to sit in a sleeping-car. Surely the deficit is not due to a lack of passengers.
Moreover, the seats are not occupied by the employees since there is only one conductor and two assistants for a train of eight to ten cars, and the conductor has to deal with all sorts of people from La Tuque to Parent, and in Abitibi. In fact, most of them are lumberjacks, and we know that they work very hard cutting wood in the forest. Normally, they could relax while travelling to visit their girl friends in their respective towns or villages. So it happens that the train is full of lumberjacks who, most of whom wait for hours in small localities such as Sanmaur, Parent and others, for the train comes at one or two o'clock in the morning. During that time, while waiting for the train from six at night to one in the morning, they hit the bottle and they are often fairly tight when they finally board the train, so that the conductor finds himself in a pretty nasty spot. The conductors have presented reports on the matter and have simply asked the C.N.R. to put constables on the train to help because they seem to have great difficulties in keeping order.
The situation is somewhat paradoxical, since the train is the only means of transportation for many of the people in the area, and I wonder why this situation is allowed to continue.
There is also another point which is most important. If there really is no place on board the trains, why not run more of them for passengers and why, especially, not make
Canadian National Railways a distinction between the various passengers? For instance, I have seen with my own eyes the ridiculous situation where a mother accompanied by several children had to sit in the middle of a "gang", as we say, of lumberjacks and I can tell the house it is no fun to hear swearing around you when there are young children. Indeed, there is another situation which is little short of ridiculous.

When funds are requested to assist the Canadian National, I don't balk of course, since they are needed. But on the other hand I would like some consideration given to the possibility of improving adequately the services in need of improvement.

In the Ottawa area for instance, where 45 per cent of the population is French speaking, is it acceptable that sometimes the conductors speak only English? I would not mind if we were in a purely English environment, but it is a well known fact that 45 per cent of the people in the Ottawa area are French-speaking. And these things are still going on.

The Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was saying recently in reply to a question from my colleague, the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin), that we never had it so good. I am tempted to say that it must have been zero formerly and two times zero is still zero. Even if the situation is twice as good or ten times as good as it was in the beginning, if it were zero, the product would still be zero. Therefore, we must ultimately have some real proof that things are going to be straightened out.
I am rather reluctant to bring up once again the matter of bilingualism. We know that in the opinion of many Quebecers, those who speak of such things today are moss-backs, old fuddy-duddies. People imagine that we are still fighting for bilingual cheques, money or stamps. Naturally, this is a huge joke in Quebec, but anyway, I wish to point out those strange situations.

Canadian National Railways Here is another example of bilingualism aboard C.N.R. trains or within crown corporations. Now, if such a situation should arise in the Vancouver or Toronto area, it is easy to imagine the reaction of a Toronto or Vancouver citizen who could not make himself understood in English by the train officer. But this is what we have been suffering for years. This is, I think, what we had to bear unfortunately, because as I said, the federal members of Quebec have always been too long in office. They thought that this could give them some advantages. But we know what has been the result of this.
Today, for instance, in the course of the debate on Air Canada and on the base that must be transferred from Winnipeg to Montreal, the cabinet members of Quebec and of the Montreal area have practically not been heard to defend their own interests categorically and energetically. We are always dealing with this famous compromise and this is why we are always full of complexes.
We are proud of only one thing. We have developed a complex of superiority which makes other people laugh, in my opinion. Here is that complex of superiority: We understand them when they speak English but they cannot understand us. Is that a complex of superiority? Certainly not, Mr. Speaker, because whoever thinks like that is so weak that there comes a time when he must find some reason to appear strong.
Therefore, the material situation of the C.N.R. in Quebec should be given special consideration. The statistics I have date back a few years-unfortunately I do not have current ones-and I have no way of knowing if the situation has changed. In the largest province of confederation, the second with regard to population, it would only be normal to find the longest railway line, in miles. That would be normal since geographically, ours is the largest province. However, Quebec has only one eighth of Ontario's railroad mileage. We are not spoiled in that respect. This material situation must change if Quebecers are to be better served.


As far as the French fact is concerned, the situation is being corrected though there are still unilingual English-speaking employees on trains serving completely or almost completely French Canadian areas.
Mr. Speaker, I am not making these few remarks to complain about discrimination but to throw light on the problem, so that everyone can consider it objectively, as it is.
If we speak of economics, let us be logical all the time, and before concluding I will remind you of a few illogical situations. Changes are sometimes made in the railway service to reduce deficits, so they say. I agree with that up to a certain point. But when the Canadian National Railways decide for instance, to abolish the position of station-master in Saint-Casimir and that according to the figures for the last few years, the net amount of profits in that station has increased steadily, one begins to wonder what is going on. It is a profit-earning station, statistics prove it, but we are told that there are no profits. Such a state of affairs makes one wonder why should it always be the same people, the same places, the same areas, that get the worst of it on account of the decision to recuperate money, while elsewhere, it is clearly acknowledged that a deficit is acceptable for this or that reason.
Of course the purpose of a crown company is to serve the public and I admit deficits may be tolerated in some areas for very definite reasons. Such deficits cannot be avoided in the field of public service, but when an enterprise is profit-earning, hands off. That is what I had to say, Mr. Speaker.

He paid $20,000 for each one of those ships, which had cost $1.2 million to build.

DEBATES	November 14, 1968
the government for. It sold its ships at a ridiculous price instead of allowing the transaction to take place in Canada. Thus it allowed a few men to get rich at the expense of the nation. Millions of dollars were wasted during a depression, at a time when Canadians did not even eat three meals a day.
That is why we are asking questions today concerning the moneys to be provided. It makes us think, because we do not know exactly for what purposes these funds will be used. There was no lack of supplies in the thirties, and yet Canadians could not eat three meals a day. When war came in 1939, the government found a way to raise the money required to pay for the greatest carnage ever seen. Today, when we are asked to authorize Her Majesty to grant loans directly to Air Canada or to guarantee issues of Air Canada securities to the tune of 130 million, we can surmise that Air Canada has to cover a deficit in its operational reserves for the period ending on June 30, 1969.
The hon. member for Beauce, Mr. Rodrigue) referred a while ago to the transfer of the Air Canada overhaul base from Winnipeg to Montreal. subtopic: PASSPORT APPLICATIONS, JAMES EARL RAY
speechtext:
That an order of the house do issue for a copy of all applications and/or other documents leading up to the granting of a passport and/or passports to Mr. James Earl Ray, the alleged assassin of Martin Luther King.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a request for the production of two applications which must have been completed by one James Earl Ray and one or two other people in relation to two Canadian passports which were found in the possession of the accused at the time he was arrested and taken to the United States by the proper authorities.
The first question which might be asked is, why do I feel this information should be forthcoming? I have in my hand an application for the issuance of a passport. As all hon. members will agree, a passport issued to a Canadian citizen arms that individual with identity not only in his own country but, with proper documentation, the right to enter other countries throughout the world. It is a very important document. In certain spy rings documentations are forged, including passports of various countries. Therefore the
November 14, 1968

issuing of a passport to a Canadian citizen is very important because a passport is one of the most important documents issued to any of us during our lifetime.
In examining the application form, which has been very carefully prepared by the department, we find that the information required includes proof of the individual's name, date of birth, identity, place of birth, height, colour of hair and eyes, weight, occupation and visible distinguishing marks. An applicant is also asked about his marital status. If the applicant was not born in Canada he must show proof of Canadian citizenship. A passport is then issued to a Canadian citizen, as I understand it, after he has signed a declaration. A declaration of a guarantor must also be completed. This is usually completed by a person in a certain category

a solicitor, a notary public, a member of parliament or a clergyman. That individual guarantees that the facts disclosed in the application are correct and that he personally knows the applicant. He then takes a solemn declaration in accordance with the law.
I might say for the record that perhaps too many of us do not analyse these documents carefully until a matter such as the one now before us comes to our attention. If the guarantor happened to be a solicitor such as myself the declaration would state: "I, Eldon Mattison Woolliams, declare to the best of my knowledge and belief that the statements made in this application are true."
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
That is the first point. Whoever made the declaration in respect of the passport application of James Earl Ray must first have declared-and this is a very serious matter- that all the statements made by the applicant were true to the best of his information and belief. In order to make such a declaration one must have knowledge of the applicant. In other words, such a declaration is not made lightly. The person you go to see is generally your solicitor, clergyman or member of parliament, a person you know and who knows you. People in this category make declarations in respect of applicants for passports; they declare that they have known them for a number of years.

subtopic: PASSPORT APPLICATIONS, JAMES EARL RAY
speechtext:
The hon. member says that a member of parliament is not included now. He used to be. Some members of parliament,
Passport Applications
like myself, are also solicitors and we are in a dual capacity. You declare that you have personally known the applicant for a number of years. Two years is the minimum. It used to be much longer. You specify the time you have known the applicant. Usually the declaration is made by somebody who has known the applicant for ten years. After you have sworn that you know the facts contained in the application are true and you have known the applicant for at least two years, you sign the declaration and it is attached to the passport application. A photograph of the applicant is also included in the passport application. The person making the declaration must certify that the photograph is that of the person making the application.
What are the facts in this regard? We are told by the C.B.C. what happened in this case. We were not told by the government because we cannot get this type of information from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner). I do not know why we cannot get this type of information from him, but that is the situation. I do not know why he would want to hide it. We cannot get this information from the Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith). Perhaps they are so cautious about giving information that even if it is not harmful it is not given to us.
We have not been able to obtain from the government information as to who actually signed the declaration or how many applications were made. But the C.B.C. tells us that two applications were made. We know that the person who obtained these two passports, James Earl Ray, has been charged in the United States with the assassination of Martin Luther King. James Earl Ray is an escapee from a penitentiary in the United States. He entered Canada legally or illegally, and after getting into this country he made an association, female or otherwise. I am certainly passing no judgment so far as she is concerned because I do not think she enters into the picture except in a social way. She knew this person and probably felt sorry for him. We know that many of these fellows can con people. They look like ministers of the cloth, but when you find out their character you realize what they are.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, this man came into Canada and met somebody unknown, also an American. They were probably connected through one of these crime syndicates we have been talking about. The deal was made. This matter is not before our courts. James Earl Ray stands charged in the United

November 14, 1968
Passport Applications
States with the assassination of a Nobel prize winner who did a great deal to bring together the two races in that country. There is some suggestion that Ray was merely there as a bluff for somebody else and did not commit the act of which he is charged. However, that will all come out in the trial to be held in the future. I see that he has now changed solicitors. But that is not the complaint I am making, Mr. Speaker. My complaint is that here we have a Canadian or Canadians, two of them, who made a solemn declaration, first that they knew that the facts contained in the application for passport were correct and, second, that they had known this person for two years and knew him to be a Canadian citizen.
When we asked questions of the Solicitor General and the Minister of Justice in respect of this matter we received the same kind of answers as we received in respect of Hal Banks. We now find out that two passports, not one, were involved. We have found this out because you can get more information from the C.B.C. than from this government. It appears, as I say, that two passports were obtained by this man. Section 10 of the act requires a commissioner to take an affidavit to satisfy himself that the deponent's signature is genuine, and then personally to administer the oath to the deponent. It provides for a fine up to $500, and not less than $25. That is in the statute.
It is difficult to obtain information from the Solicitor General or the Minister of Justice. They are great buck-passers. If the question is a little difficult for the Solicitor General to answer, he says it is not within his jurisdiction and is a question for the Minister of Justice, and vice-versa. Sometimes they throw up their hands and say they do not have jurisdiction to deal with the matter. The Minister of Justice is responsible for justice in Canada, but laying charges under the Criminal Code is the function of the attorneys general of the provinces. I will come to grips with that problem in a few moments.
The fact that a crime has allegedly been committed by one or two Canadians with reference to this application is a serious matter. It means that perjury has been committed or a false declaration has been made in contravention of the Criminal Code of Canada. I will read the relevant sections of the Criminal Code in a few moments. I would have thought that the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General, whose function it is to administer justice in this country, would have
[Mr. WooIUams.l
made sure that the most serious charges were laid in respect of completing an application for a passport, knowing the facts contained therein to be wrong, in order that a gangster of another nation could take advantage of the passport. This is why I have been asking questions about the matter; it is not that I hold any brief for James Earl Ray. People throughout the world had a great deal of sympathy for Martin Luther King. However, I am talking about the administration of justice. This is my great concern, as it is that of most people in the world wherever they may live.
To the service of criminal justice, the great concern of men on earth, we must bring the best and most dedicated talents among us. This is why the responsibility for the administration of justice in this and other countries is supposed to be given to men who rise above party politics. Such men are appointed to this position if they have these qualities to administer the law of the country. Under our system it falls to the party in power to appoint such a man. When a man is appointed to this position he is supposed to devote himself to the welfare of the citizens of the nation and rise above partisan politics. These people we must train and perfect. We must bring out the best in all who serve. The direct impact of police, judges and corrections officers on the well-being of every Canadian increases steadily because we live together to a greater degree than ever before. We cannot afford less than the best. We must engage in a continuing conversation, a free interchange of experience. Effective co-ordination among all agencies is necessary, and research and development should be available for every criminal justice need. Surely, Mr. Speaker, this is the very least we can hope for from a minister of justice.
What is the situation here? I repeat that two declarations were made by two guarantors who swore falsely-they must have- about the facts contained in the passport applications. They could not truthfully say they had known this man for two years because during some of this time he was incarcerated in the United States.
Someone has suggested that a travel agency may have been mixed up in this matter. If travel agencies in Canada are completing such declarations to obtain passports for people, then this is putting a heavy responsibility on the personnel of the Department of the Secretary of State.

Now I should like to come to the reason I want this information. Let me ask this question: How did Ray get the two passports? We know that the people in the passport office are overworked and that there are too few of them. So far as members of parliament are concerned we all agree that the people in the passport office are very helpful when we ask for special privileges for constituents who want the procedure expedited so they may go overseas to visit their relatives. When we submit an application in the morning we often get it back in the evening. The people in the passport office do a tremendous job which they perform with the degree of responsibility one would expect from public servants. But they are overworked; they receive thousands of applications which they do not have time to process properly.
How did James Earl Ray get these two passports, and what about the two false declarations? Who are these people who have not been charged either with perjury or with making a false declaration? These two men have not been charged by those responsible for the administration of justice in this country. I do not think this is a flimsy matter because here we have a man who is charged with taking the life of a Nobel prize winner, a foreigner and a gangster who came to Canada and obtained two Canadian passports. If we are going to take this lightly what will happen to the administration of justice in this nation under this or any other government? Will Canada slowly drift into the carelessness of the United States where lawlessness is rampant rather than the rule of the law, which we respect and which is for the protection of our families? If we relax our rules in this regard we let down the administration of justice.
I read with great interest the article in Maclean's magazine about the great reformer, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). He was not in the house very long before being catapulted into the prime minister's chair. He did not bring about any reforms when minister of justice, and I am not criticizing that, but I read the other day that he was a great minister of justice. I suppose he was great because he was silent; at least, we did not know what he was doing. The present Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) has already received acclaim in Maclean's magazine which says that he will be a great reformer-not jam today, jam tomorrow. We have had some great ministers of justice in this nation from the two national
Passport Applications
parties. I can think of Mr. Lapointe who had the respect of every Canadian of whatever political philosophy, and others such as Mr. Fulton. Whatever we may have thought about them they were men of integrity who wanted to see the law enforced properly.
Why were these charges not laid? The flimsy excuse has been given that one man has been charged under the commissioners of oaths act of the province of Ontario under which people wrongly issuing a passport or signing an application for a passport for a gangster from the United States are fined $25. What is the position of the Department of Justice in this regard? Is it the minister's fault, or whose fault is it? Let us take a serious look at the Criminal Code of Canada. Section 112 reads as follows:
Everyone commits perjury who, being a witness in a judicial proceeding, with intent to mislead gives false evidence, knowing that the evidence is false.
Such a man is guilty of perjury. Then we have other sections with regard to perjury, false declarations, false affidavits and false oaths under examination for discovery in the presence of officers of the court. Then we have section 113 which reads as follows:
Everyone who commits perjury is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for 14 years, but if he commits perjury to procure the conviction of a person for an offence punishable by death, he is liable to imprisonment for life.
Of course section 114 will have to be brought up to date but it shows how serious it is to take a false oath when giving evidence at a trial, whether civil or criminal. Perjury is a very serious offence if you make a solemn declaration under oath knowing that your statements are false, and particularly if you induce an officer of some department of the government to do an administrative job such as somebody did for this man. I am not suggesting for one moment that the minister has anything to hide-surely he has not-but I cannot understand why he would not get up and say, we will file those two documents and we will give this information to the opposition, whose function it is to do their job and find out facts from the government. This is all I am doing. It is my responsibility to see that the government is doing its job.
In this case I do not think the government is doing its job and I do not think the minister is doing his job. I know that the minister is a busy man, but once this matter was brought to his attention he should have said, as graciously as I would have thought he

November 14, 1968
Passport Applications
would-I have always found him to be a gracious and nice man-certainly we will find these two documents and if there is a need for an investigation we will ask the police to interview these two people or one person, whatever may be the case, with regard to the application. Is there anything to hide? I do not know why the government is frightened with regard to these things, and it is not the only government that has shown such fear; I have seen ministers from other parties do it also.

As I see it, that section applies to the making of a solemn declaration that all the facts about the application are known to you and also to the declaration that the applicant has been known to you for at least two years. Whoever completed that declaration in this case told a lie, first, that the facts in the application were true-it is a lie because the fellow was not resident in Canada and was not a citizen-and, second, that he had known the person for at least two years. It is not likely that he did know him for two years, and if he did this only compounds the crime because James Earl Ray had just escaped from a penitentiary.

(a)	signs a writing that purports to be an affidavit or statutory declaration and to have been sworn or declared before him when the writing was not so sworn or declared or when he knows that he has no authority to administer the oath or declaration,

[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
I have referred to sections 112, 114, 116 and 118 of the Criminal Code and made a differentiation between those sections which apply to persons making false statements under oath or swearing a false oath in connection with judicial matters, and other matters which are not judicial. The latter reference applies to the matter before us. As a member of parliament trying to do a job, I would have hoped that when I asked, that these documents be filed the documents would have been filed. If the documents show two people signed, different people who signed affidavits or declarations, then that is a question for the law officers of this nation, both federal and provincial, to look at in the light of the sections of the code, and lay the appropriate

charge. This is the course that should have been adopted, rather than laying a little summary conviction charge under the Commissioner of Oaths Act. If this newspaper article is true, that is what should have been done. I have no information other than would be revealed in the documents, and that is why I am asking this minister now to file the documents so that I may learn the facts. There may be more to this matter than I can see; and if there is, why cannot members learn about it?
We have been told that because the matter is before the courts it is impossible for us to have these documents. We have been told that the matter is sub judice. This rule only means that we should not say anything to prejudice the accused. It is not an umbrella for the government to hide behind, and say that they do not have to disclose these documents. Rules are to be used for the protection of people and are not intended for the government to hide behind. The government should make these documents available so that we can find out the names of the persons involved. Is this going to prejudice the accused? Is it going to prejudice the accused in connection with this particular charge?
These documents should be filed because investigation may reveal that other charges should be laid. Then a member of parliament who is doing his duty, taking his responsibility, could bring the matter to the attention of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) who, in turn, could bring it to the attention of the appropriate officers and a proper charge could be laid. I want to ask this question: What is the Minister of Justice hiding? Why does he put me in the position where I have to debate this motion, when he could have merely filed the two documents? I want to draw just one analogy, and then I am through. Since there is a new administration in the United States, today I asked the Minister of Justice whether he, through the proper diplomatic channels, would ask the new administration when they take office to review the political or administrative decision in respect of Hal Banks. I must apologize now, Mr. Speaker, for the fact that I was born and raised in British Columbia, and lived there all my life except for occasional forays into eastern Canada. As a consequence, I did not have much opportunity to learn the French language. The simultaneous translation system was not functioning from French into English while the hon. gentleman was speaking, so I heard only the last part of his remarks. He seemed to be saying that this matter is before the courts and is therefore sub judice. Eventually, the information will become public. In view of that fact he asked the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) to withdraw his motion. This is the sense of what I got from his remarks.
I am not speaking for the hon. member for Calgary North in this situation, but I believe this is precisely what the president of the

Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) said on November 6 when this matter was raised. The hon. member for Calgary North did not agree, and the matter was transferred for debate. I presume the same answer will now be forthcoming.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
There are two or three matters that disturb me about this situation, Mr. Speaker. One is whether or not this case is sub judice. Another is the proposition that was put forward by the hon. member for Calgary North, that on the surface-and there has not been any argument about this to the contrary-there are instances of somebody having signed a passport application as guarantor in a false manner; that there is here an element of somebody having perjured himself or having signed the passport application knowing that his declaration was false. This, Mr. Speaker, at least from what we have been able to find out so far, is factual and correct; certainly no one has argued to the contrary.
That being the case, Mr. Speaker, and since this question has been a matter of public knowledge for some time, it seems to me that the law officers of the crown, or the attorney general of whatever province might have jurisdiction in the case, should have been seeking out the individual or individuals who may have signed such documents in order to lay appropriate charges against them.
If, Mr. Speaker, law officers of the crown or law enforcement agencies are, in effect, going to disregard the possibility that someone might have perjured himself or made a false declaration, thus commiting an illegal act, then all this does is to help bring the law into disrepute, to treat it as nought. Surely if there has been a false declaration and a criminal act committed by whoever signed as guarantor, then such situation should be dealt with as a separate matter by the law enforcement agencies. But to hide under the proposition-as I submit is the situation-that the matter is before the courts is, I think, disregarding the consequence to which I have referred.
I do not know, Mr. Speaker, what exactly is before the courts here. All I know is that this is what the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) said the other day, as reported at page 2481 of Hansard:
The Minister of Justice has already informed the house that this case, involving a passport application to which my hon. friend has referred, is now before the courts. The matter is therefore sub

judice at this time, but we expect that the documents in question will become public knowledge-
-during the court case.
I do not want to enter your field, Mr. Speaker, of making a ruling as to whether or not a matter is before the courts or is sub judice. However, I do submit that if the President of the Treasury Board, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), the government, or the minister's parliamentary secretary, who again just raised the issue whether this case is sub judice, were really serious in their contention, then the President of the Treasury Board should have raised this point the other day, should have made the necessary order, and this debate should not have been permitted to proceed in any manner at all.
In Beauchesne's fourth edition, Mr. Speaker, there are two references in the index to matters being sub judice. One refers to citation 149 and the other to citation 152. I will deal with citation 152 last because I do not think it is the citation that applies; it alludes to references to the commissioner of taxation, the board of railway commissioners, to judges or the judiciary by way of a personal attack upon the individuals holding those offices; it does not make reference to the issue whether or not a certain case is before the courts.
However, Mr. Speaker, citation 149 does make such reference, where it states:
Besides the prohibitions contained in standing order 35, it has been sanctioned by usage both in England and in Canada, that a member, while speaking, must not:-
(c) refer to any matter on which a judicial decision is pending;-
This citation, Mr. Speaker, does, I think, refer to matters that are sub judice. If the government were serious in putting forward a case to show why these documents should not be produced in response to the motion now before us, then the government should have proceeded further and protected the rules of the house by arguing on a point of order that the matter should not be proceeded with in this manner. The mere fact that passing reference only was made to this point, and this not by way of a point of order, is really an admission on the part of the government that they do not have a sub judice argument.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, what we have is simply an over-infection of the secrecy complex that has been so evident during the current parliament. I suggest there has been an overreaction on the part of ministers of the crown to the declaration of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), that if there are any cabinet leaks

the minister responsible will lose his job; that if there are any conversations conducted by cabinet ministers with members of the press gallery or others concerning internal matters or matters brought before caucus, then heaven help the individual, he will no longer be a cabinet minister. I am sure that the President of the Treasury Board, normally a very generous and helpful minister, is thinking along this line and has interpreted, I submit in a wrong way, the Prime Minister's edict about secrecy. The course adopted does, I submit, reflect this secrecy concept of government, that things that normally should be revealed are not revealed.
I am not going to embark upon a discussion of whether or not we should be secrecy oriented or oriented toward the public disclosure of matters, unless the situation demands otherwise. The fact that the government did not bother to argue the matter procedurally under citation 149 is, I think, an indication of how shallow and shaky is their ground for claiming that this matter is before the courts and sub judice.
The other aspect to which I referred, Mr. Speaker, which was the continued lack of assiduousness in prosecuting or ferreting out individuals who apparently make false declarations, indicates the government's condoning of an act that tends to disregard the full force of the law, and thereby participates in the process of bringing the law into disrepute. After all, Mr. Speaker, if the government does not prosecute persons who make false statements of this kind, then others of like mind who seek to get a passport by false means may be able to do so with impunity, as a result of which our whole process of law would tend to break down. The simple exposure of documents to parliament and to the public would assist immeasurably in promoting proper enforcement of the law.
