speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF
speechtext:
I am pleased to have the opportunity of presenting the Customs Tariff resolution to this committee. I presume that hon. members have before them, as I have, a copy of the ways and means budget resolution of October 22.
As you will have noted, Mr. Chairman, the tariff resolution is a formidable affair of some 195 pages. I think it is fair to say, however, that the committee's task in examining this massive resolution should be less onerous than might appear at first sight. This is because the first ten sections, comprising 150 pages, represent the reintroduction in this parliament of proposals which were placed before the twenty seventh parliament over a year ago, and which were subjected to detailed examination in committees of that parliament, either the committee of the whole or the finance committee, and in fact have been in force on a provisional basis for some time.
In this connection it will be recalled that in the budget speech of October 22 the Minister of Finance referred to three sets of tariff resolutions which had been tabled by his predecessor in the last parliament, and which he was reintroducing. Probably it would be well for me to repeat, now, part of the explanation which the minister provided then, for it is relevant to this stage of our discussions.
The first set of resolutions involves for the most part what might be described as housekeeping tariff amendments. They were introduced originally in the budget presented on June 1, 1967. They reappear as sections 1, 2 and 3 on pages 4 to 8 in the general resolution before us. I believe the three resolutions just mentioned were considered in the committee of the whole in the last parliament.
The third, and by far the largest, of these sets of resolutions were those tabled on November 6, 1967, implementing Canada's commitments, other than those on chemicals
November 14, 1968

and plastics, under the Kennedy round agreements. The rates set out in these resolutions came into effect on a provisional basis on January 1 of this year. They were referred to the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs and after a series of public hearings the committee recommended them to the house for favourable consideration.
Parliament, however, was dissolved before any of these resolutions could be enacted. An order in council was therefore passed on April 25 under authority of section 22 of the Financial Administration Act, continuing in effect the proposed reductions in duty. The Minister of Finance announced at the time that collections of the increases in customs duties proposed on a few imported products were being suspended, but that it was the government's intention to ask the next parliament to enact legislation implementing both the reductions and increases, effective from the dates originally proposed in the resolutions. The resolution now before the committee will, if enacted into law, have this effect.
Those sections of the resolution which begin on page 153 relate to chemicals and plastics. They are new in the sense that they have not previously been before the house, and in that they are to come into force not later than January 1, 1969. As the Minister of Finance pointed out in the budget speech, they flow from the Tariff Board report on chemicals, under reference 120. The first volume of the board's report was tabled in this house in June 1966. The revised volume formed the broad basis for our Kennedy round negotiations on chemicals and plastics.
During the Kennedy round negotiations Canada undertook to introduce the concessions offered on chemicals and plastics not later than July 1. It was not, in fact, possible to implement the proposed new chemical and plastics schedule by that date. Accordingly, it was agreed with our trading partners that Canada could delay putting these concessions into effect until not later than January 1 next. It was also agreed, as an interim measure, that Canada would make reductions in the rates of duty on a number of chemicals and plastics in terms of the present tariff nomenclature. These were made by order in council for the period July 1 to December 31.
As to the tariff structure followed by the board, the industry proposed and the board recommended the adoption of the so-called Brussels nomenclature for most of its new tariff schedule. Both the industry and the board considered it was particularly suitable
Ways and Means
in a field of such complexity as chemicals and plastics. This nomenclature is used by the major trading countries, with the exception of the United States; it is a system for classifying goods under headings which are grouped into chapters and sections.
An integral part of the Brussels nomenclature are rules and notes which clarify the scope of the various headings. The board recommended that these rules and notes be adapted for Canadian use and that the Customs Tariff provide that the governor in council may prescribe such rules and notes. This is provided for in section 12 of the resolution on page 153.
When the tariff items relating to chemicals and plastics were referred to the Tariff Board for study the board was directed not to make any general changes in preferential margins- for example, in the difference between the British preferential and most favoured nation rates of duty. Generally speaking, at the time the board submitted its report chemicals of a kind produced in Canada were subject to duty at 15 per cent British preferential and 20 per cent most favoured nation, and those not produced at rates of free B.P. and 15 per cent M.F.N. Chemicals moved from the "made in Canada" category to the "not made in Canada" category or vice-versa on the basis of administrative rulings by the Department of National Revenue.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
The schedule proposed by the board is very long. On an extensive list of chemicals produced in Canada identified by name, the recommended rates were 10 per cent under the British preferential tariff and 15 per cent under the most favoured nation tariff, with rates of free British preferential and 15 per cent most favoured nation on a number of residual tariff items providing for chemicals not produced in Canada. The structure proposed by the board, particularly with regard to the British preferential tariff, would be less flexible than the present tariff.
As the minister said on October 22, the board's proposals have given rise to many representations urging a less rigid system, and it seemed to the government that both the present flexibility and the results intended by the board could in fact be achieved. Accordingly the resolution proposes that a 10 per cent British preferential duty, instead of the free rate proposed by the board, be established for certain items in chapters 915, 928 and 929 of the schedule beginning on page

November 14, 1968
Ways and Means
155. Under section 11 parliament is being asked to grant authority to the governor in council to lower this duty from time to time. This authority would be similar to that set out in the Customs Act to reduce or remove duties on articles used in Canada manufactures.
A somewhat similar situation exists with regard to certain plastics. Here also, in the light of additional information brought forward after the report on reference 120 was received, the Minister of Finance decided to depart somewhat from the board's recommendations, as was explained in the budget speech, in order to meet representations to the effect that the board's proposals provided no assurance of protection when new products are made in Canada.
I should like to make only three points regarding these modifications. First, they are within the scope of the Kennedy round commitments negotiated at Geneva. Second, they succeed, I think, in meeting in large part criticisms which Canadian chemical producers made about rigidities inherent in the board's original draft schedule. Third, they are consistent with the intent of the board's recommendations.
I referred earlier to the fact that the Kennedy round tariff resolution was examined, and favourably reported on, during the last session of parliament by the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs. I had the honour of being chairman of that committee during its hearings on these Kennedy round tariff changes. I would like to pay tribute at this time to the members who served on the committee during those hearings, for their serious study of the changes and their courtesy and co-operation at that time.
In its report that committee recommended the subject matter of the resolution to the house, subject to these comments. I should like to inform the house that the government has taken positive action on these suggestions, and I should like to comment briefly on each of them before resuming my seat.
The first comment or recommendation of the committee's report to the house was that great care should be taken in drafting Canadian legislation based on the new international anti-dumping code, and that the antidumping bill be referred to the committee. Both parts of this recommendation have been acted upon, and I have no doubt that the house will shortly receive a report on this

matter from the standing committee on finance.
The committee's second comment related to non-tariff barriers. Dealing with non-tariff trade barriers is, of course, a long and difficult task but, as recommended, the government has and is intensifying its efforts to deal with and counteract any adverse effects on Canadian trade from present and future barriers of this sort. To this end we have sought and obtained the co-operation and help of Canadian producers and exporters.
In its third comment the committee recommended that close attention be paid to the operation of the adjustment assistance and the machinery programs to see that their aims are in fact being met. I am glad to report to this committee of the house that in respect of each of these programs the record to date appears satisfactory. As regards the adjustment assistance program a matter for particular gratification is that as yet no one has made out a case for assistance on the grounds of serious injury, or the threat of serious injury, as a result of Kennedy round cuts in the Canadian tariff. There is now every reason to expect that it will not be necessary to use the $10 million authorized for direct loans to assist in cases of injury in the current calendar year. On the other hand, a substantial number of applications have been approved, or are under active consideration, relating to technical assistance or loan guarantees in connection with projects to modernize or expand Canadian productive facilities to take advantage of new or enlarged export opportunities.
The machinery program appears to be operating smoothly, and to the general satisfaction of Canadian users and manufacturers of machinery. In view of the concern which was expressed in some quarters last fall about administrative problems inherent in the program, it is remarkable and reassuring that it now seems to be taken almost for granted. The Minister of Finance has informed me that apart from participating as a member of cabinet in the consideration and approval each week of a machinery remission order proposed by his colleague, the Minister of Industry, he now seldom receives comment on the program.
There are, however, two aspects of the program about which I should like to say a word. The first is the matter of appeals, which was discussed at some length by the finance committee in January. Provision was
November 14, 1968

made that recommendations of the machinery and equipment advisory board may be appealed by a dissatisfied party to a review board, which will be set up if and when required. However, to date no requests for such appeals have been received, and consequently no review boards have had to be established.
My other comment relates to the scope of the program, what is included in it and what is excluded. In this connection you will recall that its scope was defined largely in terms of machinery and equipment which formerly were classified under 18 pre-existing tariff items. During the past year the predecessor of the Minister of Finance, the present Minister of Finance and also the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, have received a number of representations regarding the scope of the machinery program, some suggesting that it be expanded to include additional kinds of machinery, and others suggesting that certain products be excluded from it. They decided not to propose any changes at this time. However, it is their intention that the program be reviewed from time to time in the light of developments. Changes may be proposed in some future budget, if deemed desirable in the light of domestic and international considerations.
This concludes my remarks at this stage, Mr. Chairman. If it is your wish to call each of the 20 sections of the resolution individually, I will be glad to add further comments on each section as it is called, either at this stage or later stages of debate, comments on what these tariff changes will mean and have already meant to the positive development of Canada's trade to what I think is the general benefit of our country.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance has outlined the general intent of the resolutions, which deal with certain propositions introduced in the June 1 budget of last year and also on November 30. Fundamentally the meat of the thing concerns the Kennedy round discussions. He mentioned that parliament was dissolved and as a consequence threw the gearing of these things out of kilter. It certainly was dissolved. We find all these things are heaped up. I am quite serious when I say this government is trying to indicate that we are not getting enough business done, but here it is trying to shoulder all this stuff, which goes back to June 1, 1967, into one brief fall session. However, sir, the opposition still has some rights in this house.
Ways and Means
I would comment on one other statement the parliamentary secretary made. He was chairman of the committee at that time. He made a very able chairman and I would like to compliment him on his conduct during those committee hearings. Indeed, I think he was the most able chairman with whom I ever served on a committee. But as a consequence of having sat on that committee I am sure he will appreciate that I personally still have some reservations, and I think honestly so.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Having said that, I should like to suggest that as a result of these lengthy committee hearings last January I sincerely hope the Kennedy round adjustments will mean freer trade for Canada, and that trade will not be all one-sided. Canada should not only be importing more from outside; it should be exporting more to other countries.
The parliamentary secretary said that the Kennedy round neglected to take into consideration non-tariff barriers, which to me are most important. Let me give one small example. As I understand it, the United States copyright act is much more severe regarding productions going into the United States than our Copyright Act is in respect of productions coming into Canada. This situation must be considered seriously. My understanding is that the United States copyright act is almost prohibitive, so far as Canadian productions are concerned.
I have not been a member of the committee since it began studying the white paper on anti-dumping, which was produced by the government, but I gather that the proposed anti-dumping amendments will provide less protection to Canadian industry than now exists. At least the evidence points to this situation. The new anti-dumping legislation is not going to protect our industry to the extent it is now protected, and under the conditions which now exist we have cause for complaint.
We have heard certain rumblings, and 1 assume it is safe to say that is all they are at the moment, from the other side of the border which we'must consider of interest in respect of this whole Kennedy round procedure. Other countries and nationalities are interested in this, but in view of our tremendous trade with the United States-and I admit this is a two-way street-we must face the fact that more products come into this country than go to the United States. This is what disturbs me.

November 14, 1968
Ways and Means
It is my hope that when the Kennedy round suggestions are finally implemented we will have greater export trade, or an export trade equal to our import trade. We have heard reports emanating from our great neighbour to the south that the United States will not be happy about the implementation of some of these Kennedy round adjustments.
I trust there will not be any retaliation in this area.
It is not my intention to say anything further at this stage. As the parliamentary secretary has said, there are many pages in this budget resolution. I could not deal with them all in detail at this time. We shall wait to see the bill when it is presented. Let me again express my sincere hope and prayer that this measure will accomplish what the Canadian government thinks it will accomplish, although I have some personal reservations.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF
speechtext:
On this occasion, Mr. Chairman, looking at the resolution based on the Kennedy round, I think it is appropriate to point out the great opportunities opened to this country as a result of free trade. Let me point out also the great dangers inherent, unless we are prepared to take a number of steps in harmony with trade liberalization.
This party has always favoured a freeing of international trade in the interests not only of this country but those of the international community. We believe that the liberalization of trade will bring the nations of the world closer together, enabling us to join in opportunities in the future. The concern felt on this side of the house under present circumstances arises from the fact that to a very large extent Canadians are not masters in their own houses, so far as industry is concerned. Much of our industry is under United States domination, with the result that we have less opportunity to pursue foreign markets than we might have. The capital and know-how which has come our way from south of the border has not been priceless. This has not been just manna from above, but has been accompanied by serious implications affecting our sovereignty, and our ability to be productive.
When we consider raw materials we must obviously realize there has been little or no problem in the past. The raw materials exported by Canada have generally entered the countries of our major buyers either free of duty or with relatively little duty. In the United States particularly, where many of our raw materials are needed, the situation

has been such as to permit the entry of large quantities of our natural resources. This situation will not change very much as a result of the present situation.
Our real difficulty arises because of the nature of secondary manufacturing in this country and our inability to ship these goods around the world. Lower tariffs in themselves will not solve the problem. Nor will free trade in itself provide a solution. This is true particularly because our industry is dominated by international corporations whose purpose is to serve the best interests of the corporate structure, rather than the best interests of this country. This means that even where opportunities exist for export we are not always able to take advantage of them because a corporation may find itself in competition with one of its branches in a foreign country.
The Watkins task force, commissioned by the government to look into this matter of foreign ownership and its effects, has pointed out the very great dangers inherent in foreign ownership of industry. The suggestions it made to the government have not been followed. The task force suggested several things the government has not seen fit to accept.
It might be instructive to look at some of the areas in which we have had either free or liberalized trade, in order to see what has happened under free trade circumstances. One of the areas worth examining is the farm machinery industry. We have had free trade in respect of farm machinery for a long time. What has happened as a result of free trade? Canada was a great manufacturing nation of farm machinery. We had every reason to believe that we could become even greater and that the balance would tip in our favour. Instead of that, over the period in which there has been free trade in farm machinery our exports of farm machinery have been about one-third of our imports. We have not really benefited substantially from free trade. If we look at the figures for 1963 we see that the exports in that year were $104 million as against $293 million for imports.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
There was recently a strike at one of the plants of a very large Canadian manufacturer of agricultural equipment. The question involved was that of wage parity. The argument of the company was that it could not meet wage parity with the United States, for a number of reasons. One of the arguments of
November 14, 19G8

the company was the lower productivity in Canada. The company commissioned a report by a reputable firm in the west. That report was supposed to document the company's position as to why in this country they could not meet wage parity with the United States.
This was after many, many years of free trade. One would have assumed that the free movement of goods back and forth across the border would have meant that wage parity could have been achieved, because there was no reason for lower productivity in Canada vis-a-vis the United States. If it had been a question of difference in transportation costs, the people involved were quite prepared to accept this as one of the limitations, but the problem went away beyond just the question of transportation costs.
A Canadian who read the report prepared for the company, and their arguments, must have felt enormously depressed because of what companies such as this had done to the Canadian economy. In effect, they had concentrated all their modern plants, their automated plants, in the United States during the free trade period, and they had concentrated all their labour intensive plants in Canada. They were simply saying to Canadians: You will either accept lower wages than those of American workers, or we are not interested in locating our plants in Canada. They were saying, in effect:	You must permanently
accept a lower standard of living and give us a premium, or we are not prepared to invest further in this country and bring you up to the same level and standard as American workers.
This is a shocking indictment of free trade in the farm machinery industry-and this was a Canadian company. This plainly illustrates how much importance can be attached to the integrity of the owners of such companies. It is a shocking indictment of what happens under free trade. I bring this matter to the attention of hon. gentlemen opposite so they may realize that free trade is not a panacea in itself, that unless we have active government intervention in our economy, unless there are specific guide lines to international corporations in this country, every Canadian will be the loser. Free trade will not automatically give us a higher standard of living or even a more rational structure unless the government makes an effort to ensure that these companies operate in the long term, best interests of Canadians.
If we have to pay a bonus for each of the industries operating under free trade, the lib-
Ways and Means
eralization of trade will prove to be a disaster to this country. If we stop and think about it for a moment, we will understand why they are exacting this bonus. When an investor has a choice of obtaining a return in his own country as against a similar return in another country, even assuming that both countries have stable governments, are politically compatible and their laws are reasonable, he asks for a premium to move outside his own area of political jurisdiction. Since much of this industry is becoming more and more oriented to the United States market and to the needs of American corporations, that premium will be asked of every industry in this country operating under free trade, if left to its own devices.
Let us look at the oil industry. It is sometimes pointed out that the rationalization of the oil industry in the west has been of great benefit to Canada. I think some doubt must be expressed about just how beneficial it has been. We are still a net importer of oil. Much of our productive capacity is running away below its potential. In some areas this industry is running at about 35 per cent of the capacity of our wells. We are still importing oil, rather than having our wells operate at the volume at which they are capable.
An arrangement has been made between Canada and the United States for the movement of oil back and forth across the border, but this arrangement has been largely dictated by the needs of the international oil companies to suit their purposes and their interests, and to some extent to suit the foreign policy interests of the United States rather than the specific interests of Canada. It is my understanding that in respect of the policy we now have regarding oil there was some very substantial, behind-the-scenes arm twisting. This was during the period of office of a Conservative government. I understand that we obtained whatever arrangements we have at the moment only by threatening to build a pipe line to Montreal. The threat of building a pipe line to Montreal and taking Canadian oil at that point was one of the ways in which we got the oil companies to give us larger entry quotas into the United States. But even those entry quotas into the United States carried a price tag on them. We then had to take offshore oil, under agreed conditions, at the port of Montreal. Despite the precarious nature of these arrangements we still have a deficit in trade in respect of oil, of all things.
Let us consider another product with regard to which Canada is supposed to have

November 14, 1968
Ways and Means
an enormous advantage in terms of production. I refer to nickel. Recently there has been a shortage of nickel, which has affected foreign as well as domestic users. Our domestic producers were not able to get enough nickel for their own use. At that time increased shipments of nickel were being made out of the country in raw form. It was quite apparent-and there is on the record a statement to this effect by the then minister of trade and commerce-that the needs of the foreign buyer for raw material would be met first before the needs of the Canadian manufacturer; that this was really the No. 1 priority of the Department of Trade and Commerce.
In the long run this policy has meant we have been condemned to be sellers of raw material and to be obligated to deliver raw material rather than develop in this country our own secondary industry. What I have said about nickel is probably equally true of copper in periods of shortage. I believe the time has come when with regard to products of this type the Canadian government must establish priorities and stabilize prices for our industry, in order to stimulate and encourage them in the secondary processes of raw materials. Under free trade this will not happen.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
In recent years, since the introduction of the Canada-U.S. auto agreement, the government has taken great pride in pointing out the increased export of automobiles and parts to the United States under that agreement. Yet in this area also, while admitting there has been some improvement in the balance of trade in respect of automobiles and automobile parts, progress has not really been very rapid. Many of the advantages that we hoped to gain from this agreement have not been fully realized. Consumer prices and production facilities have not increased as rapidly as they should have, and we had every reason to believe that both of those things should have happened. I believe there are reports in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce which indicate that under this agreement productivity in Canada is as high as in the United States. Again there is a tremendous resistance on the part of the automobile companies, which are almost entirely American, to grant wage parity in Canada; and even if this were done, the fact that the value of our dollar is somewhat lower than the value of the U.S. dollar indicates that we are
a long way from wage parity with our U.S. neighbour.
With regard to trade with the United States, we find that according to the 1967 figures respecting motor vehicles and parts we still have an imbalance of trade with that country amounting to almost half a million dollars. This is an enormous imbalance of trade, and although it is somewhat better than it was a few years ago we are a long way away from reaching the objectives which we felt we were entitled to reach. The difficulty in the Canadian economy is that so much of the development that goes on in this country is designed to meet the best needs of international corporations, usually U.S. corporations, rather than the best needs of the Canadian people. I believe we have a right to say to these companies: We are happy to have you in this country and we think there are opportunities, but there are opportunities for us as well; we believe you can do well but you have to recognize our best interests at the same time as you are here making your profits. Surely this is not too much to ask. Yet when we take a look at the range of government policies, there is very little in them to move industry in this direction.
A while ago there was some talk of voluntary guide lines. At the same time it was said they would be completely useless. There was also some talk of perhaps improving those guide lines, but to what extent we do not know. Yet I believe we should not be talking in vague generalities about guide lines. This government should know what the needs of the Canadian people are, they should know what the problems are-everybody else seems to-and they should insist that we get the best arrangements possible to fulfil the needs of this country. Free trade could very well result in the loss of industry or the slowing down of industrial development in this country. It is unfortunate but true that much of the industrial development that has taken place in this country has taken place because of the tariff structure. Whatever can be said about the tariff structure, it still must be said that it has had the effect of inducing some industrial development that might not have taken place otherwise. This is not to argue for the retention of the tariff structure which I think runs counter to modern thought and the long term needs of the country, but it is to point out that that tariff structure did serve some purpose and its removal could create grave dangers.

November 14, 1968

Recently I received a letter from an industry in my area which had anticipated that certain manufacturing facilities would be set up in this country. Following the conclusion of the Kennedy round and the implementation of legislation flowing from it, that industry which spoke of locating here does not now think it is necessary to do so. It believes now that it would be just as easy for them to ship from their head office in the United States.
Free trade in itself is not an answer, and I believe Canada needs what the Watkins report called a new national policy. There was a national policy in this country years and years ago, and whatever its defects may have been it did serve to create this nation and to form the general outlines of Canada. I should like to read from the Watkins report what it has to say about a national policy:
The old National Policy served Canada in its day, as an instrument of nation-building and a means of facilitating economic growth. The challenges have changed and a new National Policy is required. The nation has been built, but its sovereignty must be protected and its independence maintained. A diversified economy has been created, but its efficiency must be improved and its capacity for autonomous growth increased.
What should those new instruments of national policy be? One of them, as suggested by the Watkins report, is a Canada development corporation, a corporation owned by the people of Canada that would step in to fill the void that exists in many areas and would ensure that much of the future growth and development of this country is in Canadian hands. The Watkins report called for a state trading agency to ensure that we do not lose sales to overseas countries because of United States policy, and of extraterritorial procedures of the United States.
We really do have a state trading company now in Canada, but it is not being used for that purpose. I think the Canadian Commercial Corporation could really do the job if it were given proper terms of reference. We have to be more willing to use crown corporations, to make up for the deficiencies of international corporations, and to challenge these corporations when they do not act in the best interests of this country. We should use adjustments boards to try to rationalize much of the industry in this country that finds itself in difficulties. Some of the industry that will be hurt will not be able to reorganize itself on an individual basis. It may be that these individual companies may have to be organized within the framework of the
Ways and Means
entire industry, and assistance and encouragement would have to be given to an industry to develop a more rational and efficient structure than is the case at present.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
But above everything else, Mr. Chairman, this country must have full employment policies. Unless there are full employment policies, the adjustment will be difficult and crucial, particularly so in some areas of Canada that are now suffering higher than average unemployment. Under full employment many possibilities exist and the stresses and strains of moving into modern ways, of accepting the challenges that are inherent in freer trade, can be met. But when you have higher than necessary unemployment as exists in this country, free trade might have the effect of exacerabting the situation. Therefore, I think it is equally incumbent upon the government, when it is talking free trade and introducing resolutions regarding free trade, to indicate to us that they will introduce full employment policies.
It is difficult to ask for this kind of commitment from the parliamentary secretary, particularly so when the Minister of Finance has recently brought in a budget that negates any attempt at full employment. The minister's budget, in the face of this resolution, has been a disaster. It is as though he had no idea that such a thing as free trade were going on; it is as though he had no idea of the problems that might be created under free trade conditions; as though he closed his eyes and turned his back on the problem before him.
However, this House of Commons will during the debates in the coming days try to focus the nation's attention on this problem, and to indicate that while we welcome the increased opportunity for reduction of tariffs around the world, we are very much aware of the other policies that must be concurrent with such liberalization of trade. We intend to press for such policies.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF
speechtext:
When we are engaged in a discussion of trade policies and tariff policies, Mr. Chairman, I think perhaps it is appropriate to say something about the immense trading potential which exists in the Pacific rim nations. Those of us who come from British Columbia, owe a great deal of our prosperity to our bourgeoning trade with Japan and other nations in the Pacific. We are perhaps, more conscious of the growing potential of trade with the Pacific rim nations than are the people of some other provinces in this

November 14, 1968
Ways and Means
country. We are aware of the vast potential, and we want to remind other people in Canada that while trade with the United States is very important, and while trade with Europe is very important, while it is appropriate to discuss matters such as the ultimate creation of a North Atlantic free trade area, we must not forget the great potential of the Pacific. We must adopt progressive trade policies in respect of nations occupying positions on that vast rim, a rim which contains nations which represent trading potential even greater than that of Europe.
I know there are Canadians concerned with the competitive aspects of trade with nations like Japan, but in the view of most people who live in western Canada-British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Alberta-a vigorous effort should be made to develop even greater two-way trade with Japan and other Pacific nations. Canadian-Japanese two way trade may pass the $1,000 million mark this year. It appears inevitable, and this may come as a surprise to some members, that it will be only a few years before Japan replaces Great Britain as our second largest trading partner.
We in western Canada have found an outlet for many of our mineral products in the booming Japanese market. Yet, at the same time, we are aware of the fact that we have no monopoly on that Japanese market. While, we can congratulate ourselves on the great two way trade in which Canada and the Japanese nation are now engaged, we, as Canadians, must be concerned about the future of that trade. There are some Canadians who believe that Japanese trade holds out a great threat to Canadian jobs and the economy of our country. But I would remind this house, Mr. Chairman, that not only have exports to Japan been continuously growing to the benefit of British Columbia, Alberta and the western provinces-yes, and to the east as well-but they have always exceeded our imports from Japan by the rate of about three to two.
Reviewing these exports we find that grains, especially wheat and foodstuffs, make up one third of the total. Metals and metallic minerals, with copper ore leading, and uranium, the most important newcomer, make up one quarter; and lumber and pulp and paper make up a further sixth. Thus, these commodities form 75 per cent of our exports. It is interesting to note that included in the remaining 25 per cent are manufactured
[Mr. PerraultJ
goods such as machinery, books and pharmaceutical products. Potash for fertilizer, which is important to our friends in Saskatchewan, is already an addition to our list of exports, and oil is another important product.
The statement has been made that since Canada's exports to Japan are predominantly raw materials, with wheat the largest single item, few jobs are created by this trade. Some of us in the west have attempted to contradict this sort of propaganda with respect to Japanese trade which comes from some other parts of Canada. This restricted view of Japanese trade and jobs may be true -as far as it goes, but it hides much of the job-creating effect of, for example, agricultural production. The actual sowing and reaping of wheat may require the labour of relatively few people, but wheat production requires materials produced in many other industries which give rise to further employment. For example it requires machinery for preparing the ground, sowing the seed, cutting and threshing the crop.
Wheat production also requires the use of fertilizer, transportation and storage as well as the use of banking facilities. Labour is needed to supply each of these factors and, to go back one stage further in the process of production, more labour is required to build the factories to manufacture the machines, and so on. Thus the total labour, direct and indirect, needed for wheat production is considerable, when the labour required at each stage is added up. A recent survey placed at over 75,000 the number of Canadians directly required to produce the whole of Canada's exports to Japan. And there are many other jobs associated indirectly with this valuable trade.
We in western Canada want all Canadians to know what this developing trade has meant to us in terms of prosperity. One of the reasons the west is one of Canada's most rapidly growing regions is because we have always had an open attitude toward trade. When we hear people in this house talk in terms of high tariffs and protectionism, adopting the attitude that we cannot lower tariff barriers because somehow it may endanger our economic security, we in the west simply say we have been competing in world markets for years. We have been selling our goods in non-protected world markets while we have had to buy many of our manufactured products from tariff-protected eastern industries. Let me assure you that in the process we have been competing very successfully, and we are doing very well.
November 14, 1968

Most people in western Canada, regardless of political party, now believe that Canadian technology, Canadian ingenuity and Canadian inventiveness have reached the stage when we can compete very successfully with many of the so-called sophisticated economies in this world. When we hear people in this House of Commons say: "Be careful about touching those tariff barriers; it may endanger jobs", we tell them, Mr. Chairman, that one way to become more competitive and to provide larger incomes for our people is by realizing the economies of scale that are possible only if we have larger markets in which to sell Canadian products. That is the key. If Canadian industry is able to sell in world markets expanded because tariff barriers are not as high as they are at the present time, we will have longer production runs and more productivity per worker. This is one way to increase the incomes of the people of this country.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
While long term contracts and joint financing provided by the Japanese have been responsible in large measure for the prosperity of British Columbia's mining industry and other industries in western Canada, Canada is not the only source of raw materials. This, Mr. Chairman, is a fact that we in this house and the people of the country must realize.
For example, Mr. Chairman, there are significant developments in Australia. That country now provides 40 per cent of Japanese coal requirements, while Canada provides 5 per cent-although the new coal contracts will improve our share of this market. Although Canada represents a large potential source of iron ore for Japanese industry, we have no automatic market there. Some people think we have. India, Chile, Malaysia, Peru and Australia are major suppliers. India supplies 21 per cent, Chile 16.9 per cent, Malaysia 11 per cent, Peru 9 per cent and Australia 7 per cent. In the year 1966, the last available figure, Canada supplied only 3.4 per cent.
The immediate future, Mr. Chairman, is one of increased competition for this country in regard to Japanese trade, perhaps a smaller proportion of the market between now and 1975, from 1.9 million tons of iron ore this year to 1.4 million tons seven years from now. Competition will become tougher because our rivals are investing in handling equipment and port facilities that can accommodate the new generation of mammoth ocean freighters.
Ways and Means
It is to be hoped, Mr. Chairman, that the government will continue to accelerate its efforts to improve ports in western Canada in order to help not only this nation but especially the products of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia to find easier and more efficient access to markets in the Pacific.
Canada is in a position, Mr. Chairman, to sell larger amounts of copper and other minerals to the Japanese market. Today the two commonwealth countries of Canada and Australia supply about one third of Japan's need for copper concentrate. Again, Mr. Chairman, competition looms in the form of Chile and the Philippines.
The point is that the Japanese market is vitally important to all Canadians. Many products that the Japanese have been able to purchase from Canada have been the result of two way trade. Yes, and they have spent money in Ontario and Quebec buying sophisticated equipment of various types. Some of the equipment has been computer equipment. All sorts of materials are being purchased in Ontario and Quebec with the dollars earned by the Japanese through their sales to Canada. That is why western Canadians say that this trade is vital to all of Canada.
Although the Japanese market is important to all Canadians, Mr. Chairman, it cannot be taken for granted; and neither can trade with the rest of this vast Pacific market. Early this year a group of economists met at Tokyo to discuss Pacific trade and development. Papers were presented by Japanese, American, Australian and New Zealand representatives, each of whom set out the role and objectives of their respective countries in the matter of developing Pacific trade. At this conference Canada was represented by three outstanding economists, one of them from Carleton University here in Ottawa. They were the well known Harry Johnson; Ted English of Carle-ton and Bruce Aitkinson of the University of Alberta. Conferences of this kind can be of immense importance to Canada, Mr. Chairman, and are deserving of the close attention and co-operation of this government.
In western Canada, Mr. Chairman, we believe that we should not divert all our attention to the north Atlantic free trade concept, or the North America free trade concept or the Caribbean area free trade concept when we talk of increasing our trade. Let us not merely send delegations down to South America, as important as those delegations are. Let us send a team of government

November 14, 1968
Ways and Means
representatives and representatives from the western and eastern provinces to make a tour of the Pacific rim. Let us send people from Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and B.C. to find out what kind of potential exists there for trade with Canada.
Under discussion at the Toyko conference- some hon. members know about this-was the possibility of at least an informal Pacific free trade area, a free trade area with vast implications for Canadians. At the January conference our Canadian representatives presented, in part, arguments that the Pacific area is one of the great potential areas for the Canada of tomorrow; and our representatives found some arguments in favour of this informal free trade concept.
Any Pacific free trade area, at least in the immediate future, would at first involve Canada, Japan, Australia, New Zealand and the United States. This would be the nucleus. Let us not back away from this concept. Let us not say that somehow it will endanger our sovereignty or that it will destroy Canadian industry. Let us not adopt these introverted, narrow, tunnel vision concepts of trade.
In the kind of world in which we live today, Mr. Chairman, there is no point in scowling at the rest of the world, in saying that we will keep tariff barriers so high that we cannot even see over them. The world is becoming smaller and smaller. It is a world where interdependence will be the key to the future. We have to develop interdependence with the nations that rim the Pacific. They must not be regarded as mysterious lands that have no potential for the products that we in Canada produce. We must not regard it as an area that can take only our basic raw materials, because I do not believe that Canadians want to be hewers of wood and drawers of water exclusively. We are in a position not only to provide raw materials of all kinds from all parts of the nation; we are also in a position to produce sophisticated equipment and the products of secondary industry. We should develop our secondary industry and accelerate exports of them as much as possible.
Canadians, Mr. Chairman, are going to become more and more familiar with the progressive, industrial giant that is modern Japan. We are going to become more and more familiar, I hope, with the potential of the Pacific. Taking Japan as an example, no other country points the way so strongly to the great opportunities for Canadian trade in

the Pacific area. No other country has developed greater initiative toward freer trade in the whole Pacific area. We should joyously and generously enter into discussions to find out how to promote that trade to our mutual benefit.

The old number of the item I am referring to is 409(f) in schedule A. For some reason or other the numbers have been changed and the new item number is 42711-1, found on page 6. -the governor in council be given authority to waive, reduce or restore these duties. This procedure will permit a shortening of the list of statutory tariff items in the plastics schedule.

What I am proposing would be the fairest and best, all things considered, including the desirability of not adding to the rate of increase of prices and costs of production.

Ways and Means
One of three principles that has been recognized by the parliament of Canada for many years is that farm machinery or equipment should enter this country free of customs duty and excise taxes. I should like the support of hon. members from the prairies on this matter. I ask the government and the parliamentary secretary whether the government intends to follow this premise; will it allow farm machinery or equipment to be used on farms free entry into Canada. Most farmers, and I am sure most hon. members in this house, believe that the provision for such an intention of parliament has been provided for under schedule A, which I referred to a few moments ago.
Among other items in schedule A is found this wording:
All other agricultural implements or agricultural machinery, n.o.p.
For the benefit of hon. members who do not know the meaning of those letters, they stand for the words, "not otherwise provided". I take it that that ought to cover all agricultural machinery and implements not provided in the foregoing-and there is a great big list here.
Officials in the Department of National Revenue for some reason do not agree with this interpretation. They have power to impose duty on those items, which I am sure parliament intended to allow in duty free. The difficulty or controversy arises from the interpretation of two expressions, the first of which is "agricultural machinery", and the other "agricultural implements".
I think most of us will admit that in this day and age there is not one piece of machinery, or any one implement that is used on the farm that could not be used for some other purpose, if the need arises. This is the point that the officials seem to be trying to stress. When an application is submitted to them, the officials challenge the entry of the item that is applied for on the grounds that it could be used for some other purpose. They do not allow it to enter duty free.
I ask, does the minister believe in the principles he enunciated in the three statements I referred to a few moments ago? Does he believe in the desirability of not adding to the rate of increase of prices and cost of production, and the shortening of the list of statutory tariff items? I suggest to the parliamentary secretary that both the minister's principles would be served and justice to the farmer would be served if there were a slight change

Ways and Means
in the wording of the tariff I have referred to.
I suggest that where the wording now is, "agricultural implements" and "agricultural machinery, n.o.p.", it ought to be changed to read, "all equipment, apparatus, ^ machines and implements for agricultural use".
If the parliamentary secretary will agree to that change I shall sit down and save the time of the committee. Otherwise I shall continue with my remarks. Perhaps the parliamentary secretary might indicate now whether he accepts my suggestion.

I am sure the explanation given by the parliamentary secretary will not be looked on with favour by the farmers of Canada. This is not a new item. The piece of paper I have in my hand is over 20 years old, and farm machinery was allowed duty-free into Canada at that time. However, there will be plenty of time in which to continue this discussion. I am more than ever convinced that I have to try to impress on the government and on members of this house the need

to get this one item changed under 409F, or at least to get some definition of the terms used upon which everyone will agree.
Am I right in my assumption that it was, and is, parliament's intention that agricultural machinery and implements intended for farm use be allowed into Canada duty free? I contend I am right in making such an assumption. X shall refer again to schedule A. I have read the item which refers to agricultural implements and machinery. For many years the people of this country assumed there was no difficulty whatsoever about getting agricultural implements into Canada duty free. I say it was the intention of parliament in those days that they should be admitted duty free, and that this intention has not changed.
I will refer the committee to items 409N 409-0 and 409-Q. These items all refer to goods which are allowed entry into Canada free of excise tax and customs duty. Item 409-0 refers to equipment for generating electric power when used for farm purposes only. On the basis of these examples it won;cl seem to me that the intent of parliament was obvious j it was to assist farmers to keep down their cost of production so that they could compete in world markets. In case the minister or the parliamentary secretary should charge us with failure to make representations to the government on this matter at an earlier stage, let me point out that this issue has been raised on several occasions. Ways and Means
Finance should clarify what it is doing in making these changes. The Department of Finance puts these items in, and God knows who will be able to interpret them afterwards. The Department of National Revenue cannot do so. The Tariff Appeal Board cannot do so. When cases go before the courts, the judges have a heck of a time interpreting what is meant.

From time to time when discussing definitions in this house we have suggested that the Department of Finance recommend one dictionary that it will use, if there is dispute about any change in a word or about interpretation of a word. The department has refused to do that. When it is making these tariff changes I want those responsible to spell out what they mean by "agricultural machinery" and "agricultural implements" and, Mr. Chairman, I intend to stay on my feet until I get them to do that.
The parliamentary secretary was talking about the intention of parliament and about the idea that farm machinery and farm equipment are allowed into Canada free of tariff and excise tax. This is an erroneous statement, because as a consequence of the efforts of civil servants in the Department of National Revenue very few pieces of this machinery or equipment come into Canada free of tariff and excise tax.
As I said before, many representations have been made to the department. Recommendations have even been made by members of the Tariff Board that this entry be changed, but there has been no action from the Department of Finance.
I refer to the speech made by the hon. member for Mackenzie on July 30, 1963, as recorded at page 2813 of Hansard when he said:
The minister is saying that this is a complicated procedure-
Just like the parliamentary secretary is trying to do right now.
through which we have to go before we can get an exemption. I recall, for example, that during the war the procedure was very simple. Eaton's and Simpson's had a blank form in their mail order catalogue and all you had to do was fill out the form to indicate that you were a farmer and that the particular item you were buying was for farm purposes. This was all that was required during the time of war. This method was devised by people who were getting a dollar a year. Now, however, we find this is an extremely complicated problem and the matter cannot be looked at for another year. This does not make sense.

November 14, 1968
Ways and Means
That was five years ago, but no change has been made by the Department of Finance. I think it is high time that the government told farmers that it is not interested in lowering the costs of production of farm produce. In fact we have an example here-blame it on the Kennedy round if you wish-where the costs of production are going to be increased by the amount of the increase suggested here tonight.
My second argument that this item should be changed comes from the question, why does the government impose customs duty and excise tax on items to be imported? The obvious answer is additional revenue for the federal treasury and, more particularly, the protection of industry. I ask protection of what industry? Surely it is not just the manufacturing industry of eastern Canada? Surely the minister was not just referring to the manufacturing industry when he said he was desirous of keeping costs of production down? Knowing the minister as I know him, I am certain he had the agricultural industry in mind also when he made that statement.
As all hon. members know, both eastern and western agriculture are going through very difficult times. In fact so far as western agriculture is concerned it could be said that this industry is going through a transitional period, and the need for government protection and action is evident now, possibly more so than ever before. Evidence of eastern agricultural problems was demonstrated a short time ago when eastern farmers marched on Ottawa. I hope, as I said before, that eastern members representing rural ridings in this house will support my plea with reference to a change in this item.
Western agriculture is suffering from lack of markets for grain. It is facing the necessity of producing more competitive grades of wheat, and it is also facing the problem of increasing costs of production. By parliament today not recognizing the intent of the term, "all other agricultural implements or agricultural machinery n.o.p." we are contributing to an increase in the costs of farm produce.
Some will say, and rightly so, that the farmer has recourse from a denial by civil servants of free entry, by appealing to the Tariff Board. An action of this type is costly and in many cases more than the individual farmer can afford. As a result he pays the tax, as the civil servant expects he will. I would suggest to the parliamentary secretary that in the event a farmer won his appeal to the board, if the civil servant responsible for

forcing the appeal in the first place were assessed the costs, then more farmers would receive the justice to which they are entitled under the laws of our country, and we would be following the intent of parliament when it inserted this one item in schedule A.
If there were any doubt in the mind of the person whose duty it is to decide whether a machine or implement is to be used for agricultural purposes, an end user's certificate could be requested. However such a proposal has never been accepted, to my knowledge, by the departmental officials. At least all my efforts in that direction have been fruitless.
The principal behind such a proposal is the same as that applied by the Saskatchewan government in the use of purple gasoline. If it is used for farm operations it is not taxable. If it is used for any purpose other than farm operations the violator is prosecuted. I would suggest that the same thing should apply here. If anyone gets away with importing machinery or implements under the guise of their being used for agricultural purposes, then it is up to the government to prosecute that person if he does not use them for those purposes.
If the minister will not accept the suggestion to change the wording of the item in question, then I ask that he arrange acceptance of an end user's certificate, stating the machine or implement applied for free importation is for farm use only, and if found being used for other purposes the violator should be prosecuted.
My third reason for requesting the minister to change the wording deals with the difficulty encountered in interpretation of the present two phrases. I think the minister will agree that if the term in the bill cannot be defined, then it is serving no useful purpose by remaining in the schedule. However, I suppose they intend to leave it in the schedule. Being there it is confusing and, as a result, creates unnecessary procedures such as appeals to the Tariff Appeal Board and to the courts. This has been the circumstance for years, and parliament has made no effort to change the situation. Efforts have been made by individual members, but these have not been successful.
As I have stated, members of the appeal board themselves have stated that the terms "machines" and "implements" have an elastic connotation, and they find difficulty in determining parliament's intent. Surely to goodness if board members themselves find difficulty in interpeting the things we put into
November 14, 1968

the act, it is up to us to assume the responsibility for changing the words, so that they can understand what we mean. As I said before, if we do not know what we mean when we put these words into the act, how can we expect civil servants, or even judges, to know?
On the other hand in the only case I had time to read, the court in question gave a much broader definition to the terms than did the civil servants in the Department of National Revenue. Therefore I would suggest to the parliamentary secretary that if more farmers could afford to take their rejected appeals to the courts they would receive the benefit of the intent of parliament and the justice they have a right to expect in our society or, as the term goes now, in our just society.
Because the individual farmer has occasion only once or twice in a lifetime to make application for free entry, he hesitates to take his case to the courts, due to the cost factor. This additional cost factor he cannot afford, and this is one of the reasons civil servants in the department have been so successful in their denial of the farmer's right.
When dealing with officials of the department the farmer finds that every possible obstacle is put in his way in reply to his application. For instance, we find the following reply: "The decision is final and conclusive". Another comment used, in one of the letters I have here, is this: "There is no provision in the agricultural implements schedule of the Customs Tariff whereby pumps for use in flood type irrigation may be admitted."
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
I wish I had time to read many of the precedents outlined by civil servants in the department for the farmers. I should like to know at this time what is a precedent: Is it something that supports what the department is saying or is it something that supports what I am saying? Having regard to the nature of some of these letters, I think someone should be taken to task.
I wrote the Minister of National Revenue on September 16, as I have done on several occasions, objecting to the very definitely negative paragraphs put out by some of his officials and sent in the form of farm letters to my constituents. I said that the civil servants should endeavour to assist rather than
Ways and Means
hinder those who contribute to their maintenance. I suggest one of the tasks of civil servants is to help these constituents.
The officials give yet another reason for rejecting these applications, saying in one case that the equipment must be of an active rather than a passive nature. They use this reasoning when a farmer is trying to get a wagon box exempted, saying that it must be of an active nature. A wagon box, of course, has no working parts. When you try to get a pump exempted, I presume they come back and say that it must be of a passive rather than an active nature. Apparently these precedents can be used both ways.
I have been surprised to find that many of these cases taken to the appeal board have been decided in favour of the farmers, after it was proved that the machinery involved could be used to a great extent not only for farm purposes but for other industrial uses. If farmers could afford to take their cases to the appeal board I think they would get much better satisfaction.
Let me put it to the parliamentary secretary, that this procedure is unnecessary if parliament would change the wording to which I have referred, making it much easier for the courts to make a decision. I should like to go into everything the courts have said in respect of agricultural machinery, in order to give members of this house a better idea of the problems the farmers have been facing when they make these applications. Let me refer to one case I found, which dates back to June 22, 1954, and is found in volume 1 of the Tariff Board Reports, at page 316. The president of the Exchequer Court in his judgment said:
It is, therefore, important to ascertain the ordinary meaning of the term "agricultural implements". If the defendant's friction disc sharpeners come within such meaning it is not necessary to consider the ambit of the term "agricultural machinery". The word "agriculture" is defined in the New English Dictionary, vol. 1, as follows:
'the science and art of cultivating the soil; including the allied pursuits of gathering in the crops and rearing livestock; tillage, husbandry, farming (in the wildest sense).' and "agriculture" is defined as:
'of or pertaining to agriculture; connected with husbandry or tillage of the ground.'
He continues and gives the definitions as contained in Webster's New International Dictionary, Funk and Wagnall's New Standard Dictionary, Webster's New International Dictionary-I suppose he is referring to

November 14, 1968
Ways and Means
another edition-and so on. After giving those definitions he then states:
I must now determine whether the defendant's friction disc sharpeners come within this ambit.
He concludes his judgment by saying:
It was also urged for the plaintiff that the term "agricultural implements" meant only implements that were actually used in tilling the soil or in such agricultural operations as seeding, harvesting or the like but did not include articles that were merely ancillary to such implements, such as the defendant's friction disc sharpener. In my judgment, there is no such limitation in the ordinary meaning of the term and, certainly the various classes of persons who dealt with or used the sharpeners did not consider there was any such restriction of meaning. They had no doubt that the sharpeners were farm implements, and therefore, agricultural implements. In my opinion, they were right.
I am quite sure, as I said before, that if farmers could take their cases to the courts they would win 90 per cent of them. In order that they do not have to do this I plead again with the parliamentary secretary to have the department change the wording of this one item.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to preface my remarks in respect of the Customs Tariff by congratulating the parliamentary secretary on his appointment and his able and competent chairmanship of the finance, trade and economic affairs committee during the last session. I should like also to congratulate the officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce who negotiated the Kennedy round agreements on behalf of Canada.
The parliamentary secretary said he would be pleased to answer some of the questions that might be fired at him. Perhaps he is prepared to tell us how the government feels about the attitude of the United States in respect of the Kennedy round agreements, and particularly the anti-dumping policy. Apparently there is some difficulty in this regard in Congress, and there might be problems in getting it passed.
There has also been an attitude expressed by the French government in respect of accelerating the tariff items, and this would have a direct effect not only on the European Economic Community but also on trade with France and other countries. Perhaps the hon. member is prepared to make a statement in that regard.
Every time I think of the GATT, which is the general agreement on tariffs and trade, I think of the words "fait accompli", because these items were put into effect on January 1 of this year. As of this calendar date they 
appear to be of this nature; nevertheless we have to go through the necessary steps to make them law in this country. The first question that should be asked in respect of the GATT agreement is, what effect has it had on lowering the tariffs in Canada and on the Canadian economy? This question was referred to the Economic Council of Canada, which was commissioned to make a special review of the tariff structure. That council found that the effective protection afforded Canadian industry, under the Kennedy round agreements, had not been substantially reduced, and in some cases was substantially less than before.
Let me quote from an article which appeared in the Toronto Daily Star of September 12, 1968, in which the Prime Minister rejected further lowering of tariffs. This was in direct contradiction to the recommendations of the Economic Council of Canada, that the Canadian tariff structure be reduced beyond the scope of the present Kennedy round commitments.
This article refers to effective protection and the degree to which Canadian producers could keep prices high without foreign competition. The article suggests that the impact on Canadian prices is expected to be very slight. I should say that this must be considered within the framework of the accelerated reduction of tariffs proposed by the council as one way of dealing with persistent prices which cause increased costs. The Economic Council of Canada made a special review of the Kennedy round agreements and suggested they afforded very little protection. Certainly the government did not follow its recommendations with regard to meeting the high cost of living, and the high prices that Canada is experiencing at this time.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
If Canada is to have a strong economy both in terms of its productive strength and financial structure, we must have a free trade policy. This free trade policy must be determined by our monetary policies, our trade policies and the industrial structure under which we operate in this country. Referring first to our monetary policies, one finds some restrictions imposed on us by reason of our fixed exchange rate policies and our foreign exchange reserves, which at the moment must be in the neighbourhood of $2.55 billion. When I set forth the proposition that we must take a new look at our fixed exchange rate policy and our foreign exchange reserves, members of the government will say: Here is
November 14, 1968

a New Democrat setting forth one of their wild-eyed theories.
I tell the parliamentary secretary that I am going to read to him the words of the Postmaster General in a book called "The Nation Keepers". The Postmaster General wrote an article in that book entitled "Foreign Guide Lines and Canada's Economic Future", and on page 214 of that book he says this:
If Canada pursues an aggressive free trade policy it is obvious that our fixed exchange rate policy will not work. We will have to go through so many fundamental changes in industrial organization that only a freely moving rate will be able to adjust to the productive process and measure our success or failure in achieving our aims. As J. E. Meade has written, there is no choice for free traders. "Free trade and fixed exchange rates are incompatible in the modern world." This is particularly true for a Canada which depends on trade, has a heavily protected manufacturing industry, and is much affected by the slightest changes in the economic policy of its neighbour. Freer trade will bring a more efficient use of our resources and expand our possibilities of growth, but these changes cannot possibly work their way through the economy within the constraints of a fixed rate.
The basic argument for fixed exchange rates is to protect the Canadian businessman from fluctuations in the value of the dollar. With a fixed rate he can plan; he knows what the costs of imported tools and machinery will be; he can measure precisely the net receipts from his exports. But why should the businessman be protected from risk and change? Is it not precisely the function of entrepreneurs and innovators to take advantage of economic change to control and direct the forces of change? By protecting the Canadian businessman from change, whether by tariffs or fixed exchange rates, we content ourselves with less than optimum performance and should not be surprised if our control over our economy lessens. Fixed exchange rates mean that we shape the Canadian economy to maintain an external equilibrium. For example, we are presently committed not only to maintain a fixed rate of exchange for the Canadian dollar but also a fixed ceiling to the amount of our exchange reserves. Our efforts, then, to employ more fully our human and material resources, including the 300,000 new jobs that we must find each year, must be circumscribed by these commitments. Exchange rates, which should adjust to the productive process, control and order our affairs. The whole weight of our economic policy is brought to bear on marginal problems, the problems of stabilizing a rate of exchange or maintaining rates of interest to control capital flows. We are forced to ignore the fundamental problems of growth and employment. Our balance on current account is approximately 2 per cent of our gross national product, and one would normally consider that economic policy directed to the composition and growth of G.N.P. would yield more satisfactory results than policies which have the effect of containing G.N.P. for the sake of maintaining a given balance in international payments.
These are the views of the Postmaster General with regard to the fixed exchange rate
Ways and Means
and foreign exchange reserves. One notes with satisfaction that the chairman of the Royal Bank of Canada, Mr. W. Earl McLaughlin, stated in today's Globe and Mail the same proposition, namely that Canada is hamstrung in its trade policies by reason of the fixed exchange rate and foreign exchange reserves. This is the first restriction that has been imposed upon us with regard to developing a free trade policy in Canada.
The second restriction is with regard to the industrial structure of the Canadian economy. This is why the problem of foreign ownership is so important to all Canadians. This is why the government sent forth the task force to study foreign ownership and the structure of the Canadian economy. Foreign investment in Canada as of 1964 amounted to $27 billion. As of now it is probably closer to $35 billion. Of that $27 billion in 1964, 80 per cent was American investment, 12 per cent investment of the United Kingdom and the balance that of other countries.
When one considers the Canadian economy, and more particularly automobiles, automobile parts and rubber products, being controlled by American investment to the extent of 97 per cent, chemical products of Canada being controlled by American investment to the extent of 78 per cent, and electrical parts and apparatus to the extent of 77 per cent, he can appreciate the magnitude of this problem.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it ten o'clock?
Progress reported.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-REPORTED CRITICISM BY MANITOBA SUPREME COURT JUDGE
ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-REPORTED CRITICISM BY MANITOBA SUPREME COURT JUDGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 28 I directed a question to the Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith). My
November 14, 1968

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion question arose from a decision rendered in the appeal court of Manitoba by Mr. Justice Freedman in a case in which a man, a citizen of Winnipeg, had been convicted of theft. In dismissing the case Mr. Justice Freedman expressed very serious criticisms of the handling of the case by the R.C.M.P. officers involved in making the arrest.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
I have always believed that in Canada we should follow the procedures which have been established in the United States by the supreme court of that country, under which any person accused of a crime has the right to counsel, not just at the time of his trial but at the time of his being questioned by the police. Canadian courts have never followed this procedure although it is a pretty well established principle of British justice that a person who wishes to have counsel is entitled to have it. In the case to which I refer the person accused of theft told the R.C.M.P. officer that he wished to have counsel present when he was questioned. He was on the telephone with his lawyer. The R.C.M.P. officer took the telephone away from him, spoke to his lawyer and told him that he would not delay the questioning of the accused until the lawyer got there.
I want to quote briefly, because I think it is important, from the judgment given by Mr. Justice Freedman, which reads as follows:
The facts surrounding this aspect of the case are disturbing to anyone who prizes the rights of individual liberty in a free society. Among these is assuredly the right, on being arrested or detained, to retain and instruct counsel without delay. This is a right enshrined in English common law, vindicated by many judicial decisions of high authority and clearly and unmistakably affirmed in the Canadian Bill of Rights...
Mr. Justice Freedman goes on to give the facts of the case and to quote from the statement made by the accused and by the lawyer of the accused in which the lawyer, Mr. Brock, said, among other things:
I told Constable Taylor that I wanted to advise Ballegeer not to make a statement until I could talk to him but Taylor refused. I asked Taylor to relay my advice to Ballegeer but he said he would not do so.
The judge goes on to say:
Here is a spectacle of a police officer wilfully, and alas successfully, frustrating the due process of law. What the constable did was wrong and unjustifiable, and his conduct cannot receive the sanction of the court.
I want to conclude by saying that I am concerned about this case. It seems to me that

the Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith) has the responsibility not only of investigating what happened in this case but in making certain that the R.C.M.P. officers, not just the constables doing the work but the R.C.M.P. officials at the top, understand that citizens have rights and that the law gives them rights, so that the R.C.M.P. like any other agency of government, must live by the laws and rules which we have established.
It seems to me that this is an extremely important case and one which the Solicitor General should take steps immediately to clear up in no uncertain manner.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to tell the hon. member on behalf of the Solicitor General, who is away on official business and could not be here tonight, that we have taken note of his remarks.
