maintopic: HUMAN RIGHTS-REQUEST FOR NON-DISCRIMINATION POLICY IN NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT PROJECTS
HUMAN RIGHTS-REQUEST FOR NON-DISCRIMINATION POLICY IN NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT PROJECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 29 I directed a question to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, one which arose in my mind as a result of the refusal of the Supreme Court of Canada to hear again the case of Terrence John Whitfield v. Canadian Marconi Company.
These events took place some years ago. Mr. Whitfield was an employee of the Canadian Marconi Company working on the DEW line; and Marconi was fulfilling a contract for the federal government on that line. One of the conditions of employment which Mr. Whitfield signed was a condition which I do not understand, and certainly could not possibly justify. This is a condition which all employees were required to sign, namely that there would be no fraternization between any of the employees who came from southern Canada and the native population.
Mr. Whitfield, being a young man, and human, became interested in a young Eskimo lady named Ann Witaltuk. Despite the provision of the contract he had signed, he became friendly with her. I have an affidavit signed by the young lady which indicates that on one occasion she accompanied him to a social affair at the officers' mess at the R.C.A.F. station at Whale River. In order to gain entry to

November 14, 1968

the officers' mess it was necessary to pass through a guardhouse leading to the works project. Miss Witaltuk recalls that the guard acting tor the Canadian Marconi Company, at first stopped her from entering. Indeed he stopped both Mr. Whitfield and the young lady, saying he had instructions not to allow Eskimos to enter.
To cut a long story short, Mr. Whitfield was discharged. He subsequently sued the Marconi Company and his case was dismissed. I am not going to discuss what happened, except to say that it seems to be inconceivable that the government of Canada, which was enacted a Bill of Rights, a government which has passed the Fair Employment Practices Act, at a time when most provinces have passed a fair accommodation practices act, all of which certainly enunciate one simple principle that the people of this country are opposed to discrimination on the basis of race, colour or creed, should accept this situation.
I am not trying to rehash the Whitfield case. Surely, if we believe that we cannot condone the kind of thing which happened in the Whitfield case, then I should like the minister to adopt a very simple principle, that wherever the government does business with a company, whether it is giving a contract to a company, whether the company is doing work for the government or whether the government is giving a concession for mining, oil exploration or lumbering operations, the government should make it a condition of the contract with the company that there shall be no discrimination on the job or off the job in any way at all.
It seems to me I am making a very simple suggestion, and I can see no reason why this or any other government of Canada, in the light of the opinion about discrimination, should not agree to it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (Minister without Portfolio):
maintopic: HUMAN RIGHTS-REQUEST FOR NON-DISCRIMINATION POLICY IN NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT PROJECTS
speechtext:
Concern about discrimination has been expressed by several hon. members for many years, but more particularly recently by the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Orange), the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). I appreciate the opportunity of telling hon. members some of the measures that are being taken by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development; one in the form of a directive which was sent recently to departmental employees, enunciating certain policies. I do not believe time will permit the
2777
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion reading of the whole of it, but I will read some extracts.
I begin with the following:
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
The Canadian Eskimos enjoy full citizenship, freedom, right and responsibilities as is the case with all Canadians regardless of origin, creed or colour...
Government employees are expected to treat all Eskimos with whom they come into contact either by business association or socially in a manner calculated to maintain the respect we have or should have for one another in the spirit of the Canadian Bill of Rights.
It goes on to provide for investigation and for appropriate action to be taken where such policy has not been carried out by any government department.
This policy has been brought to the attention of all departmental employees recruited to work in the north. It also requires that departmental officials will bring this policy to the attention of all agencies and contractors doing work for the department in the north.
At a recent meeting of the advisory committee on northern development it was confirmed by all government departments involved that they will accept this policy, and it was subsequently confirmed formally that they were administering this policy vigorously with respect to any contractors within their area of jurisdiction. The policy embodied in that directive-which, as I say, I could not read in toto since time does not permit-was brought to the attention of the United States government and is now incorporated in the terms of the agreement administered by contractors on the DEW line system.
I would also refer to the statement made by the Minister of Labour on November 6, as reported at page 2470 of Hansard. With regard to the employment practices of the Northern Canada Power Commission I refer to the statement made by the deputy minister in his capacity as chairman of the commission, before the standing committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development on November 5, page 3.
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION___________

Mr. Speaker, my appearance this evening arises from the program "The Way It Is" on C.B.C. television two days before the United States election, an election, sir, that I suggest was the cause of great anxiety not only to
2778	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Americans but to the friends of Americans, including ourselves.
Part of the program that evening was a journalistic essay called "Listen, America" created by a cameraman named Yves Delau-rot. It dealt with black power, with riots, with police brutality. It showed a burning Buddhist monk; it dealt with marijuana; and one scene showed many naked hippies at a love-in. Some of it, as Patrick Watson stated, was staged; but he did not indicate which portions were indeed so staged. Technically, I think it was well produced and the camera work was superb.
However, Mr. Speaker, I say of the show that its timing was poor. I say of this show that its theme was entirely one-sided and biased. Canadian Broadcasting Corporation employees in Ottawa have told me that it was obviously put into the program by an antiAmerican clique in the C.B.C. in Toronto.
I say of the show, Mr. Speaker, that its presentation was in the tradition of cheap journalism of the kind that would make the editors of Hush and Flash sit up and say: "I wish we could get away with that, but the police and the Postmaster General would not let us". I also say, Mr. Speaker, that part of this show was a play for perverts who rejoice in sadism. I say that part of the show was for those who like irregular sexual practices and obscenity.
I suppose, Mr. Speaker, that I will be met with some kind of argument to this effect: Well, after all, we must have freedom of expression. I do not have the right in our free society to go forth into the town square and shout four letter words. I do not have the right in our free society to throw ordure at another person.
But above and beyond the sheer lack of taste displayed in that particular program, or at least in that particular segment of it, I would say this, Mr. Speaker. We have had experience in parliament of dealing with the management of the C.B.C. We all recall the
DEBATES	November 14, 1968
famed expression of a former minister who said the C.B.C. had "rotten management". We have had the "Seven Days" hearings. We have had hearings ad infinitum and ad nauseam in the time I have been in parliament and before. Yet, Mr. Speaker, no cure has been effected.
It is still obvious that there is no direct link between upper management and management at the level which would put this sort of trash on a television program. There is no effective management at the top. Who are the people who planted that journalistic essay in the program? Obviously they include some in important places, at decision-making levels, whose moral outlook is depraved and whose entire outlook is one of anarchy and nihilism. No wonder the editor of the Saint John Times-Globe wrote of this incident concerning, "The way it is", under the title, "The way it shouldn't be".

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Stanbury (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of Stale):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, officials of the C.R.T.C. informed me that comments have been received about the program referred to by the hon. member. I know he understands very well that under the Broadcasting Act the C.B.C. has the right and responsibility to produce its programming free of government interference, and subject only to the law and the regulations of the C.R.T.C. I might mention, as the hon. member will know if he saw the program, that the film which he spoke about was clearly identified and introduced as a biased and one-sided presentation, and not a documentary, of certain issues confronting the United States of America.
I offer no judgment about the merits of the program. I invite the hon. member and others who are interested in it to express views to the C.R.T.C. and the C.B.C. in the matter.
